item.research_question: What is the atomic-scale origin of repeated dislocation pinning and jerky motion in concentrated random high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the absence of short-range ordering or elemental clustering?
item.material_system: Face-centered cubic (FCC) CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (Cantor alloy), plus subsystems CoNi, CoCrNi, and binary CoCr
item.processing_route: In-situ TEM tensile straining of FIB-prepared lamellae (thickness ~100 nm, loading rate controlled by step motor, 300 kV TEM); Atomistic simulations using LAMMPS with 2NN MEAM potentials, samples of ~100 million atoms with surface notches, shear loading at 5 K and 300 K, and rigid displacement GSF calculations with constrained out-of-plane relaxation
item.test_conditions: In-situ TEM: 300 kV, 50 frames/s, uniaxial tensile strain; Simulations: Cryogenic (5 K) and ambient (300 K) temperatures, shear forces ramped to 0.208 eV Å⁻¹, constant shear forces applied after critical force determination
key_findings: Dislocations in CoCrFeMnNi exhibit wavy lines and jerky glide motion via a kink-pair-like mechanism even without segregation or clustering around Shockley partials.
Atomistic simulations reproduce jerky motion in perfectly random samples, showing 'V'-shaped pinning at 5 K that straightens at 300 K due to thermal activation.
Atomic-resolution STEM EDS confirms no elemental segregation or clustering around dislocation cores, with per-column concentration fluctuations negligible compared to bulk.
The density of high local Peierls friction (FP) is proportional to the critical stress (FC) required for dislocation glide; FC scales linearly with the 95th percentile of FP (FP,95).
Dislocation mobility (M) is inversely proportional to FP,95, with a linear correlation observed between M and FP,95⁻¹.
Strong pinning points (FP ~0.8 eV Å⁻¹) arise specifically from Co atoms surrounded by increased Cr concentration, whereas Fe and Mn act as weak pinning sites (FP ~0.2 eV Å⁻¹).
The Co-Cr interaction is identified as the primary driver for strong pinning; binary CoCr shows higher pinning density than CoCrNi, and Ni is not strictly necessary for strong pinning.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that local fluctuations in the Generalized Stacking Fault (GSF) energy landscape, caused by random atomic arrangements, create spatially varying Peierls friction barriers. Specifically, unique nonlinear interactions between Co and Cr atoms generate local energy minima adjacent to high barriers, resulting in steep energy gradients (high FP) that act as strong pinning points. The density of these high-friction sites determines the critical stress and mobility, operating without the need for short-range ordering.
item.limitations: The study was conducted at cryogenic temperatures where thermal activation is suppressed; at intermediate temperatures, thermal energy may allow dislocations to overcome weaker barriers. The descriptor is based on rigid shear displacement and may not directly apply to BCC metals where kink-pair mechanisms dominate. No single structural motif was confirmed as the sole cause of pinning, as chemical coordination shows great variance.
item.future_work: The authors suggest the proposed atomic descriptor (FP) can be used for predictive materials design to tailor dislocation pinning without costly MD simulations of moving dislocations. They propose investigating the transferability of the descriptor to BCC HEAs by finding rigid shear paths for screw dislocations. Further work is implied to explore the design of alloys with increased resistance to glide onset and reduced mobility by tuning Co-Cr interactions.
quotes: We demonstrate that the density of high local Peierls friction is proportional to the critical stress required for dislocation glide and the dislocation mobility.
The interaction of Co and Cr causes the emergence of a new peak with FP values ~0.8 eV Å⁻¹ where Co atoms have become substantial obstacles for the dislocation line.
The underlying mechanism is directly linked to local fluctuations in Peierls (force/friction) barriers, which lead to dislocation pinning points in concentrated random alloys.
